timeline.event: Kenaf cultivation is traced back to about 4000 BC in ancient Africa.
India produced about 100,000 tonnes and China about 41,000 tonnes of kenaf and allied fibers, about 49% and 20% of the world total.
Field work on mining soil found that intercropping kenaf with soybean raised cadmium in kenaf leaves, a caution for fiber from polluted land.
Hydroponic work described how kenaf roots tolerate and sequester cadmium under stress.
A review grouped kenaf with hemp, ramie, jute and flax as bast crops with potential for remediation of degraded land.

timeline.event: With wartime kapok supplies cut off, the United States ran a national milkweed pod collection to fill life jackets.
A case report documented occupational asthma in a worker exposed to kapok, confirmed by bronchial challenge.
Laboratory work characterized kapok as a natural hollow, hydrophobic and oleophilic sorbent for oil.
Oil sorption of kapok, milkweed and polypropylene fiber assemblies was compared under controlled packing densities.

timeline.event: The Lusehoj Bronze Age textile from Voldtofte, Denmark, was identified in 2012 as nettle cloth, probably imported from the region of present-day Austria.
Germany expanded nettle fiber production during the First World War after flax and cotton stocks ran out, using nettle fabric for army uniforms.
Gustav Bredemann began selecting wild nettles for vigor and fiber content, founding the clone collections behind later fiber nettles.
Research on nettle fibers for the German textile industry increased again during the Second World War.
Surviving Bredemann clones were re-evaluated, restarting breeding and processing trials.
A chromosome-level genome of stinging nettle was published, including candidate genes for the neurotoxic peptide urthionin.

timeline.event: Kijoka bashofu weaving in Ogimi, Okinawa, was recognized as an Important Intangible Cultural Property of Japan.
Toshiko Taira, who led the revival of Kijoka bashofu, was named a Living National Treasure.
Researchers produced banana fiber yarns for technical textile reinforced composites, refining fiber with a pectinase bath.
Toshiko Taira died at the age of 101.
Warm-water retting of banana stems for 21 to 25 days gave fibers of about 34 cN/tex with a moisture regain of about 13.6%.
